title: Why Do I Get Drunk Faster Now? Age, GLP-1s, Meds and More
excerpt: Getting drunk faster than you used to? The real reasons: lost tolerance, age, weight loss, GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic, medications, hormones, and stronger drinks, plus when to see a doctor.
metaDescription: Getting drunk faster than you used to? Learn the real causes: lost tolerance, age, weight loss, Ozempic and other meds, hormones, and stronger drinks.
author: DHM Guide Team
tags: why do i get drunk faster now
content:
**The honest answer first:** if you seem to get drunk faster than you used to, there is almost always an ordinary explanation. The most common ones are that you drink less often than you did (so your tolerance has faded), you're older (so your body holds less water and clears alcohol differently), you've lost weight or are eating less, you've started a medication that adds to alcohol's effects, or your drinks have quietly become stronger and bigger. Newer weight-loss drugs such as Ozempic, Wegovy, and Mounjaro have added a fresh reason to that list. Usually it's two or three of these stacking at once.

A change in how alcohol hits you is useful information, not something to push through. It means the same number of drinks now puts more strain on your body than it used to. The fix is usually simple: drink less per occasion, slow down, eat first, and check your medications. This guide walks through each cause, how to tell which ones apply to you, and the signs that mean you should talk to a doctor.

> **When to see a doctor.** Most people who feel alcohol more than before have a harmless explanation. But talk to a doctor soon if the change came on suddenly without an obvious reason, if you've started a new prescription (especially a sedative, sleep aid, pain medicine, anxiety or seizure medicine, or a GLP-1 weight-loss drug), if you have diabetes and notice shakiness or confusion after drinking, or if you have new memory gaps after amounts that never caused them before. Also mention it if you notice yellow skin or eyes, swelling in your belly or legs, easy bruising, or unusual tiredness, since these can point to liver problems. **Get emergency care (call 911 in the US)** if someone who has been drinking is confused and can't stay awake, has slow or irregular breathing, has a seizure, is vomiting while very drowsy, or has cold, clammy, or bluish skin. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, and they need care right away. This article is general information, not medical advice.

## What "Getting Drunk Faster" Actually Means

When people say they get drunk faster, they usually mean one of two different things, and it helps to separate them.

1. **Your blood alcohol rises higher or faster.** The same drinks produce a higher blood alcohol concentration (BAC) than before. This is about your body: how much water it holds, how quickly alcohol leaves your stomach, how much you've eaten, and how fast your liver works.
2. **Your brain reacts more strongly to the same BAC.** Your blood alcohol might be the same as it always was, but you feel more impaired, sleepier, or dizzier. This is about tolerance, age, sleep, and anything else in your system that affects the brain, such as medications.

Many of the causes below push on both at once. Keep the two in mind, because the fix for each is a little different. If your BAC is higher, eating and pacing help a lot. If your brain is more sensitive, the only real fix is fewer drinks.

## You Drink Less Often Than You Used To (Lost Tolerance)

This is the most common reason, and the one people least expect. If you used to drink several nights a week and now drink mostly on weekends, or you took a break for a few weeks or months, your tolerance has come down.

Tolerance comes in two main forms:

- **Metabolic tolerance.** Regular drinking increases the activity of some of the liver enzymes that break down alcohol, including one called CYP2E1. A frequent drinker clears alcohol somewhat faster. When you cut back, that boost fades.
- **Functional tolerance.** Your brain adapts to alcohol being around often. It adjusts its own chemistry so the same BAC causes less obvious impairment. When you stop drinking regularly, the brain readjusts back, and alcohol feels stronger again.

Neither form of tolerance protects you. A tolerant drinker still has the same blood alcohol and the same strain on the liver and heart. They just notice it less. So "losing your tolerance" is really your body returning to an honest reading of how much alcohol you're having. That is a good thing, even if it's surprising at a wedding.

Our guide to [alcohol tolerance](/never-hungover/alcohol-tolerance) covers how it builds and fades in more detail.

**How to tell if this is you:** you cut back recently, the change feels gradual, and everything else about your health is the same.

## Why You Get Drunk Faster as You Get Older

Age changes how the body handles alcohol in several ways, and they tend to show up from your 40s and 50s onward. There's nothing wrong with you. It's normal physiology.

### Less water in your body

Alcohol spreads through the water in your body. Muscle holds a lot of water, and fat holds very little. As people age, they tend to lose muscle and gain fat, even if their weight stays the same. Less body water means the same amount of alcohol ends up more concentrated, so your BAC climbs higher from the same drink. The US National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA) points to this as one of the main reasons older adults are more affected by alcohol.

### A more sensitive brain

Older brains also seem to be more sensitive to alcohol's effects on balance, reaction time, and memory. That means even a modest BAC can affect your coordination more than it would have at 25. This is one reason falls and injuries after drinking become more of a concern with age.

### Slower processing

Liver function and blood flow change with age, and alcohol may be cleared somewhat more slowly. Some research also suggests the stomach breaks down less alcohol before it reaches the blood as people get older, though findings vary.

### More medications

Older adults are much more likely to take daily prescriptions, and many common ones interact with alcohol (more on that below). Age plus one or two medications is a very common combination behind "I can't handle drinks like I used to."

### Hangovers often feel worse too

Plenty of people notice that hangovers get rougher with age at the same time they start getting drunk faster. The two are related: higher peak blood alcohol, worse sleep, and slower recovery all play a part. We explain this in [why hangovers get worse with age](/never-hungover/why-hangovers-get-worse-with-age).

**How to tell if this is you:** you're in your 40s or older, the change has crept in over a few years, and it's more noticeable in balance and sleepiness than in mood.

## Getting Drunk Faster on Ozempic, Wegovy, or Mounjaro (GLP-1 Medications)

GLP-1 medications such as semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro, Zepbound) have become one of the most talked-about reasons people say alcohol hits them harder. The research on alcohol and these drugs is still early, so it's worth being honest about what's known and what isn't.

**What people report:** many users say they feel drunk after fewer drinks, lose interest in drinking, or feel sick from amounts that used to be fine. Some report stronger hangovers.

**Possible reasons, in plain terms:**

- **You're eating much less.** These drugs reduce appetite, and many people drink on a lighter stomach than before. Food in the stomach is one of the strongest brakes on how fast alcohol reaches your blood. Less food means a faster, higher spike.
- **You've lost weight.** A smaller body means the same drink produces a higher BAC. If you've lost a meaningful amount of weight, your old "number" no longer applies.
- **Slower stomach emptying.** GLP-1 drugs slow down how quickly the stomach empties. In theory, this could delay alcohol absorption rather than speed it up, so its exact effect on BAC isn't clear. It can, however, make nausea and stomach upset from alcohol worse.
- **Changes in how alcohol feels.** Early research suggests GLP-1 drugs may affect the brain's reward response to alcohol. Small studies have found reduced drinking in some people taking semaglutide, and larger trials are ongoing. This could change how alcohol feels, though it's not settled.
- **Blood sugar.** Alcohol can lower blood sugar, especially on an empty stomach. If you also take insulin or a sulfonylurea for diabetes alongside a GLP-1, the risk of low blood sugar is higher. Low blood sugar can look a lot like being very drunk: shakiness, sweating, confusion, and slurred speech.

If you're on one of these medications, the practical advice is the same: eat a real meal before drinking, start with less than you think you need, and wait before having another. Talk to your prescriber about alcohol, especially if you have diabetes. For the details on each drug, see our guides to [Ozempic and GLP-1 medications with alcohol](/never-hungover/ozempic-glp1-alcohol-hangover-2026-research-guide), [Wegovy and alcohol](/never-hungover/wegovy-and-alcohol), and [Mounjaro and alcohol](/never-hungover/mounjaro-and-alcohol).

## Medications That Make Alcohol Hit Harder

A new prescription is one of the most important things to check if alcohol suddenly feels stronger. Some medicines add to alcohol's sedating effect on the brain. A few may affect how alcohol is processed. Either way, the result can be feeling much drunker than the number of drinks would suggest, and some combinations are genuinely dangerous.

**Talk to your doctor or pharmacist** before drinking on any of these. This list is general and not complete:

| Type of medicine | Common examples | Why it matters with alcohol |
|---|---|---|
| Sleep aids | zolpidem (Ambien), diphenhydramine-based "PM" products | Both are sedatives. Together they can cause heavy drowsiness, poor coordination, and memory gaps. |
| Anti-anxiety medicines | benzodiazepines such as alprazolam (Xanax), lorazepam (Ativan) | Strongly adds to alcohol's effect on the brain. Can slow breathing at higher amounts. |
| Opioid pain medicines | oxycodone, hydrocodone, tramadol | Dangerous combination that can slow or stop breathing. |
| Nerve pain and seizure medicines | gabapentin, pregabalin | Can add to drowsiness and dizziness. |
| Muscle relaxants | cyclobenzaprine, methocarbamol | More sedation and dizziness. |
| Older antihistamines | diphenhydramine (Benadryl), doxylamine | Sedating on their own, much more so with alcohol. |
| Some antidepressants and antipsychotics | varies by drug | Many add drowsiness. Some carry specific alcohol warnings. |
| Diabetes medicines | insulin, sulfonylureas | Raise the risk of low blood sugar, which can mimic drunkenness. |

Some acid-reducing medicines have been studied for whether they raise blood alcohol slightly by affecting alcohol breakdown in the stomach. The effect, if any, appears small for most people, but it's another reason to mention every medicine you take when asking a pharmacist about alcohol.

The basic rule: if a medication's label or leaflet says it may cause drowsiness, assume alcohol will make that much stronger. Our [alcohol and medications guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-medications) goes through the common interactions one by one.

**How to tell if this is you:** the change started within days or weeks of starting or changing a medicine. Don't stop a prescription on your own to make room for drinking. Ask your doctor instead.

## You've Lost Weight or Changed Your Diet

Weight is part of the classic BAC formula for a reason. If you weigh less than you used to, the same drink is spread through less body water, so your blood alcohol goes higher. This applies whether the weight loss came from a medication, a new training plan, illness, or a diet.

Diet changes matter even without weight loss:

- **Intermittent fasting.** Drinking at the end of a long fast, or as part of a small eating window, means alcohol hits an empty stomach.
- **Low-carb and keto diets.** Many people on these diets report getting drunk faster. The likely reasons are less food in the stomach when drinking, lower body water (low-carb diets shed water early on), and lower stored carbohydrate in the liver. Some people also switch to spirits with diet mixers, which may be absorbed faster than drinks with sugar. The research here is limited, so treat these as likely contributors rather than settled science.
- **Skipping dinner to "save calories" for drinks.** This is one of the fastest routes to an unexpectedly high BAC.

Food, especially a meal with protein, fat, and fiber, slows the rate at which alcohol moves from your stomach into your small intestine, where most of it is absorbed. Our guide to [drinking on an empty stomach](/never-hungover/drinking-on-an-empty-stomach) explains why this single factor can make such a large difference.

## Hormones, Perimenopause, and Menopause

Women generally reach a higher BAC than men from the same amount of alcohol. The main reasons are less body water on average and, according to some research, less alcohol broken down in the stomach before it reaches the blood. We cover the differences in [alcohol metabolism in men vs women](/never-hungover/alcohol-metabolism-men-vs-women).

Midlife adds another layer. During perimenopause and after menopause, body composition tends to shift toward less muscle and more fat, which lowers body water. Many women also report that alcohol feels stronger, worsens hot flashes and night sweats, and disrupts sleep more than before. Research on exactly how menopause changes alcohol processing is still limited, but the overall pattern of feeling alcohol more is commonly reported. See our guide to [perimenopause and alcohol intolerance](/never-hungover/perimenopause-alcohol-intolerance) for more.

Some people also wonder whether the menstrual cycle changes how drunk they get. Studies on this have been mixed, and there isn't a consistent finding that one phase of the cycle reliably raises blood alcohol.

## Your Drinks Have Gotten Stronger (Without You Noticing)

Before blaming your body, look at what's in your glass. Drinks have drifted stronger in ways that are easy to miss.

- **Higher-strength beer.** A standard US drink assumes a 12-ounce beer at about 5% alcohol. Many craft beers, IPAs, and seltzers are 7%, 8%, or more. A 16-ounce pint of an 8% IPA contains roughly twice the alcohol of a standard beer.
- **Bigger wine pours.** A standard drink of wine is 5 ounces. Restaurant pours and home pours are often 6 to 9 ounces, and many wines are now 14% alcohol or higher.
- **Cocktails with more than one shot.** Many popular cocktails contain two or more servings of spirits.
- **Canned cocktails.** Some ready-to-drink cans contain the equivalent of two or more standard drinks.
- **Carbonated mixers.** Some evidence suggests fizzy mixers can speed absorption for some people, though the effect varies. Our article on [whether carbonation makes you drunk faster](/never-hungover/does-carbonation-make-you-drunk-faster) looks at the research.
- **Drinking faster.** Your liver clears roughly one standard drink per hour, give or take. Drinking faster than that, which is easy at a lively event, stacks alcohol up in your blood no matter how tolerant you are.

If you switched from light beer to hazy IPAs, or from a bar pour to your own generous kitchen pour, your "three drinks" may now be five or six standard drinks. Our guide to [how many drinks it takes to get drunk](/never-hungover/how-many-drinks-to-get-drunk) explains standard drinks and the main variables.

## Tiredness, Stress, and Being Run Down

Sleep loss makes alcohol's effects stronger. Research on sleep deprivation and alcohol has found that tiredness and alcohol add to each other's effects on reaction time and alertness. If you're drinking after a long week, a red-eye flight, or a few nights of poor sleep, you'll likely feel more impaired from the same drinks.

Other things that make you feel alcohol more:

- **Being dehydrated**, for example after exercise, sitting in the sun, or a stomach bug.
- **Being ill**, especially with a fever or infection.
- **High altitude**, where many people feel alcohol more strongly, though research on whether BAC itself is higher is mixed.
- **Stress and anxiety**, which can change your eating, sleeping, and pacing even if they don't change your BAC directly.

These causes come and go. If you get drunk faster only on certain nights, look at what those nights have in common.

## When a Change Could Point to a Health Problem

Most of the time, getting drunk faster has one of the explanations above. Occasionally it can be linked to a health condition, which is why a sudden, unexplained change is worth mentioning to a doctor.

- **Liver problems.** The liver does most of the work of breaking down alcohol. If it isn't working well, alcohol and other substances may be cleared more slowly. Liver disease often has few symptoms early on, so a routine blood test can be worthwhile if you drink regularly.
- **Diabetes and blood sugar issues.** Low blood sugar after drinking can look and feel like being very drunk.
- **Thyroid or other hormone changes**, which can affect weight, energy, and how you feel generally.
- **Neurological or sleep conditions**, where alcohol may worsen balance, memory, or breathing during sleep.
- **Gastric bypass and some other weight-loss surgeries.** These can make alcohol reach the blood much faster and cause a much higher peak BAC. If you've had weight-loss surgery, ask your surgical team about alcohol.

Some people also find they react badly to alcohol in a different way: flushing, stuffy nose, headache, or a racing heart after small amounts. That's usually alcohol intolerance rather than getting drunk faster. Our [alcohol intolerance guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-intolerance) explains the difference.

### Memory gaps are a signal to slow down

If you're having memory gaps after amounts that never caused them before, take that seriously. Blackouts happen when blood alcohol rises fast enough to interrupt the brain's ability to form memories. They are a sign your BAC got too high, too quickly. Our guide to [blackouts](/never-hungover/blackout-drunk) covers why they happen and how to avoid them.

## How to Work Out What's Changed for You

A quick self-check can usually narrow it down. Ask yourself:

1. **Do I drink less often than I did a year ago?** If yes, lost tolerance is likely part of it.
2. **Have I started, stopped, or changed any medication, including over-the-counter sleep or allergy products?** If yes, check with a pharmacist.
3. **Have I lost weight, started a GLP-1 drug, or changed how I eat?**
4. **Am I eating less before or while I drink?**
5. **What exactly am I drinking, and how big are the pours?** Check the label for the alcohol percentage.
6. **How fast am I drinking?** More than about one standard drink per hour will raise your BAC steadily.
7. **Am I tired, stressed, or run down on the nights I feel it most?**
8. **Am I 40-plus, or going through perimenopause or menopause?**

If you answer yes to several, you probably have your explanation. If none apply and the change is sudden, that's the situation to raise with a doctor.

## Practical Ways to Adjust

You don't need to fight your body's new reading. You need to match your drinking to it.

- **Reset your number.** Whatever your old limit was, assume it's lower now. Start with one drink and see how you feel after 30 to 60 minutes.
- **Eat a real meal first.** A meal with protein, fat, and fiber before drinking slows absorption and lowers your peak BAC.
- **Pace yourself.** Aim for no more than about one standard drink per hour, and alternate each drink with a glass of water.
- **Choose lower-strength drinks.** Switch to session beers, smaller wine pours, single-shot cocktails, or spritzers. Check the label.
- **Measure at home.** Use a jigger for spirits and a measured pour for wine for a week. Many people are surprised by what their "one glass" really is.
- **Don't drink on a new medication** until you've asked your doctor or pharmacist whether it's safe and how much.
- **Plan your ride home.** Feeling drunk faster also means you may be over the legal driving limit sooner than you expect. Remember that only time lowers your BAC. Coffee, cold showers, and food after the fact don't speed it up. Our guide to [how long it takes to sober up](/never-hungover/how-long-does-it-take-to-sober-up) explains why.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree, often sold as a hangover supplement. Some lab and animal research suggests it may affect how the brain responds to alcohol and may support the liver's alcohol-processing enzymes. Those findings are from rodents, and none of the small human trials looked at tolerance.

To be clear about what it can't do: there is no good evidence that DHM stops you getting drunk, lowers your blood alcohol, or makes it safe to drive. It doesn't cancel out a medication interaction or make up for drinking on an empty stomach. If you're getting drunk faster, the first steps are the ones above: fewer drinks, more food, slower pace, and a medication check.

If you'd like to try DHM for the morning after, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Check with your doctor first if you take any prescription medicine. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers timing and amounts, and if you're older, our guide to [DHM for adults over 50](/never-hungover/dhm-adults-over-50-age-related-safety-2025) covers extra safety points.

## The Bottom Line

- Getting drunk faster than before is common and usually has an ordinary explanation.
- The most frequent causes are lost tolerance, getting older, weight loss or eating less, GLP-1 weight-loss drugs, new medications, hormonal changes, and drinks that are stronger than you realize.
- Several causes often stack together.
- The fix is to lower your number, eat first, pace yourself, and check every medication with a pharmacist or doctor.
- See a doctor if the change is sudden and unexplained, came with a new medication, or comes with memory gaps, blood sugar symptoms, or signs of liver trouble. Call 911 for signs of alcohol poisoning.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why do I get drunk faster now than I used to?**

The most common reasons are that you drink less often (so your tolerance has faded), you're older and have less body water, you've lost weight or are eating less, you've started a medication that adds to alcohol's effects, or your drinks are stronger and bigger than before. GLP-1 weight-loss drugs such as Ozempic and Mounjaro are another common reason. Often two or three of these are happening at once. If the change is sudden and none of these apply, talk to a doctor.

**Why do I get drunk so easily all of a sudden?**

A sudden change usually has a recent trigger: a new medication, a period of not drinking, a diet change or skipped meal, weight loss, poor sleep, illness, or a switch to stronger drinks. Check what changed in the weeks before you noticed it. If you can't find a reason, or the change comes with memory gaps, confusion, or other new symptoms, see a doctor.

**Do you get drunk faster as you get older?**

Yes, for most people. With age, the body tends to hold less water and more fat, so the same drink produces a higher blood alcohol level. The brain also becomes more sensitive to alcohol's effects on balance and reaction time, and older adults are more likely to take medicines that interact with alcohol. This usually shows up gradually from midlife onward.

**Does Ozempic make you get drunk faster?**

Many people on Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, and similar GLP-1 drugs report feeling alcohol more strongly, but the research is still early. Likely reasons include eating less, weight loss, and changes in how the brain responds to alcohol. These drugs also slow stomach emptying, and their exact effect on blood alcohol isn't clear. Eat before drinking, start with less, and ask your prescriber about alcohol, especially if you have diabetes.

**Why do I get drunk faster after losing weight?**

Body size affects blood alcohol. When you weigh less, the same drink is spread through less body water, so your blood alcohol level rises higher. People who lose weight also often eat smaller meals, which lets alcohol reach the blood faster. Lower your usual number of drinks to match your new size.

**Can medications make you get drunk faster?**

Yes. Sleep aids, anti-anxiety medicines, opioid pain relievers, gabapentin, muscle relaxants, sedating antihistamines, and some antidepressants all add to alcohol's effect on the brain, which can make you feel much more drunk from the same amount. Some of these combinations can be dangerous. Ask your doctor or pharmacist before drinking on any new prescription.

**Does losing your tolerance mean something is wrong?**

No. Losing tolerance after drinking less is normal and healthy. Tolerance only hides how impaired you are. Your blood alcohol and the strain on your body are the same either way. A lower tolerance gives you a more honest signal of how much you've had.

**Will DHM stop me from getting drunk faster?**

There is no good evidence that DHM stops you from getting drunk, lowers your blood alcohol, or makes it safe to drive. The intoxication findings people cite come from a 2012 rat study, and no human trial has measured whether DHM changes how drunk you feel. The reliable ways to feel alcohol less are drinking fewer and lower-strength drinks, eating first, and pacing yourself.
